findings_matched.gt_title: Malicious executable p.exe in attacker staging directory
findings_matched.judge_reasoning: Both findings describe the same process (p.exe, PID 8260) and the same specific malfind observation: a 481-page RWX memory region at address range 0x2be0000-0x2dc0fff. The agent finding is more specific about the VAD details and interpretation, while the GT finding provides broader context about the staging directory and execution chain. The core observation — the large PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE private memory region in p.exe indicating a packed/injected payload — is identical in both.

findings_matched.gt_title: Attack conducted under spsql account with Domain Admin privileges
findings_matched.judge_reasoning: Both findings describe the same core observation: the spsql account (same SID S-1-5-21-3445421715-2530590580-3149308974-1193) with Domain Admin privileges and High Mandatory Level integrity being used in the attack, with PID 5848 explicitly verified in both. The agent finding is more expansive (covering additional PIDs 8260 and 8712, and noting network logon origin), but the primary subject — spsql account with Domain Admin privileges running the attacker's processes — is identical.

findings_matched.gt_title: WMI lateral movement used to access this host
findings_matched.judge_reasoning: Both findings describe the same core observation: WmiPrvSE.exe (PID 2876) spawning powershell.exe (PID 8712) at 2018-08-30 16:43:36 UTC as part of WMI-based lateral movement. The agent finding is a more detailed and specific version of the ground truth, adding the downstream process chain (WOW64 PowerShell PID 5848, cmd.exe, p.exe) and timing details. The ground truth mentions the 32-bit PowerShell C2 shell as a child of the 64-bit PowerShell, which corresponds to the agent's WOW64 PowerShell (PID 5848). The primary subject — WMI-initiated remote PowerShell execution via WmiPrvSE.exe — is identical in both findings.

Both findings describe the same network observation: multiple TCP connections from 172.16.6.11 to 172.16.4.10 on port 8080 in ESTABLISHED and CLOSE_WAIT states, with no PID association preserved. The remote IP, remote port, local IP, connection states, and orphaned PID characteristic all match. The agent finding provides more specificity (memory offsets, attribution to p.exe, slightly different connection count breakdown) but is clearly describing the same underlying observation. The C2 inference is shared by both.

findings_matched.gt_title: Six short-lived rundll32.exe instances from PowerShell C2 shell
findings_matched.judge_reasoning: Both findings describe the same core observation: PowerShell PID 5848 spawning exactly 6 rundll32.exe instances (PIDs 6768, 5452, 5588, 2216, 4108, 8148) that each lived only seconds. The PIDs, parent process, count, and short durations all match precisely. The agent finding adds additional context (p.exe spawning separate rundll32 instances, no command-line arguments) and frames the mechanism slightly differently (process injection vs. staged DLL execution), but the primary subject — the 6 rundll32 children of PowerShell 5848 — is identical. The mechanism framing difference (injection carrier vs. staged DLL execution) is interpretive rather than describing a different observable event.

findings_matched.gt_title: p.exe DLL profile confirms network-capable C2 implant
findings_matched.judge_reasoning: Both findings describe the same core observation: p.exe (PID 8260) loaded a full networking and cryptography DLL stack (WININET.dll, WS2_32.dll, DNSAPI.dll, IPHLPAPI.DLL, CRYPTSP.dll, rsaenh.dll, bcrypt.dll, Secur32.dll, SSPICLI.DLL) consistent with a C2 implant, and mpr.dll was loaded approximately 6 days after initial execution indicating continued activity. The agent finding is more specific (adds USER32/GDI32 late-load detail and includes PS 5848 as an additional subject), but the primary subject and evidence for p.exe are identical. The additional PS 5848 content in the agent finding does not disqualify the match since the core p.exe DLL profile observation is clearly shared.

findings_matched.gt_title: Outbound lateral movement via SMB and RDP
findings_matched.judge_reasoning: Both findings describe the same core observation: outbound lateral movement from this host to 172.16.7.15:445 (SMB) and 172.16.4.5:3389 (RDP). The agent finding is more detailed, including additional connections (inbound SMB, LDAP, WinRM) not mentioned in the GT, but it fully encompasses the GT's primary evidence. The two specific connections cited in the GT (172.16.7.15:445 ESTABLISHED SMB and 172.16.4.5:3389 CLOSED RDP) are explicitly present in the agent finding. The agent finding is a superset of the GT observation, which qualifies as a match.

Both findings describe the same negative observation: no registry-based or service-based persistence was found. Both reference the same evidence — empty Run keys for spsql, legitimate entries (OneDrive, Dashlane, DashlanePlugin) for tdungan, and svcscan returning no malicious services. The agent finding is more detailed in specifying exact registry paths and search terms, but the core observation is identical. Both also note the attacker likely relied on live session access rather than boot-persistent mechanisms.

findings_matched.gt_title: PowerShell (PID 8712) malfind hits are .NET CLR heap segments, not injection
findings_matched.judge_reasoning: Both findings describe the same observation: windows.malfind flagging three RWX regions in powershell.exe (PID 8712) and both concluding these are benign .NET CLR allocations, not injection or shellcode. The GT identifies the signature as heap segment headers (0xFFEEFFEE), while the agent references CLR sync structures and clrjit.dll presence — both are consistent explanations for the same CLR/JIT memory pattern. Same process, same PID, same tool, same region count, same benign conclusion.

findings_matched.gt_title: PowerShell C2 shell has AMSI loaded and multiple unnamed DLLs
findings_matched.judge_reasoning: Both findings describe the same observation: PID 5848 (PowerShell) has multiple unnamed DLLs (no name/path) loaded, interpreted as evidence of reflectively loaded modules from an attacker's framework. The agent finding is more specific, noting ~15 entries vs GT's 12, and adds detail about anomalous timestamps as a reflective loading artifact. The core subject (unnamed DLLs in PID 5848 suggesting reflective injection) is identical. GT also mentions amsi.dll being loaded, which the agent finding does not address, but the primary observation being matched here is the unnamed DLL pattern, which both findings share.

precision_note: Precision is count-based (unit weight per agent finding); recall is severity-weighted. weighted_f1 is their harmonic mean — mathematically valid but an asymmetric hybrid, not a single-scheme F1.
